definition: Random features (RF) are a technique used in machine learning to approximate kernel methods, introduced by Ali Rahimi and Ben Recht in their 2007 paper "Random Features for Large-Scale Kernel Machines", and extended by.
details: RF uses a Monte Carlo approximation to kernel functions by randomly sampled feature maps. It is used for datasets that are too large for traditional kernel methods like support vector machine, kernel ridge regression, and gaussian process.

explainer.lead: Random features is a technique that approximates kernel methods by randomly sampled feature maps, introduced by Rahimi and Recht in 2007. It matters because it makes kernel-style learning tractable on very large datasets.

tiers.eli5: Kernel methods compare every pair of points, which gets impossibly slow with lots of data. Random features replace those comparisons with a quick random sketch that behaves about the same.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers use a Monte Carlo approximation to kernel functions, applying random feature maps when datasets are too large for support vector machines, kernel ridge regression, or Gaussian processes. A pitfall is approximation error from finite random sampling.
tiers.paperLevel: Uses a Monte Carlo approximation to kernel functions via randomly sampled feature maps, introduced in 'Random Features for Large-Scale Kernel Machines' (2007) and later extended.

explainer.example: For a dataset too large for kernel ridge regression, randomly sampled feature maps are drawn so that inner products approximate the kernel, enabling linear-scale training.
